#### §3: Memory allocation

| ID | Spec | Ann. | Decision |
|---|---|---|---|
| D-3.1 | §3.1 | — | **Two allocation domains.** Library-internal memory uses the internal heap directly. Memory handed to C callers (`strdup`, `getline`, `open_memstream`, `asprintf`, `scandir`, ...) comes from the *exported, interposable* `malloc` through the PLT, so that a user-interposed `free` can release it (spec §3.3; F23). |
| D-3.2 | §3.1 | ARB, HIST | `malloc(0)` returns a unique freeable pointer. `realloc(p, 0)` frees and returns NULL. Both are the contract's glibc choices, kept for compatibility. |
| D-3.3 | §3.1 | HIST | Internal deallocation passes size and alignment (`free_sized`-style), so there is no per-block header for internal allocations. C `free(p)` recovers the size from the size-class map. |
| D-3.4 | §3.2 | HIST, COMPAT | Introspection is implementation-neutral. `mallinfo2` reports in-use, held and releasable bytes in the fields whose meaning is neutral, and zero elsewhere (observable). A block freed by another thread counts as free once its `free` has returned, collected by its owner or not (D-3.11), in every report (`mallinfo2`, `mallinfo`, `malloc_stats`, `malloc_info`): the reader subtracts pending remote frees, so the result does not depend on when collection runs. `mallinfo` saturates at `INT_MAX` instead of wrapping (observable, stricter). `mallopt` returns 1 for every parameter, known or not, as glibc (owner ruling 2026-10-22, #412), and 0 only for `M_MXFAST` outside 0 to 160; only `M_PERTURB` takes effect, the others are ignored. `malloc_info` emits the same XML element structure with neutral content. |
| D-3.5 | §3.3 | HIST | The hook variables are inert compat data (as in 2.34+). `mcheck`/`mtrace` semantics come with the debug library (phase 13). `malloc_get_state`/`malloc_set_state` fail. **Phase 13 (owner ruling 2026-10-04: kept; phase 14 ships an empty `libc_malloc_debug.so.0`, and preloading it gives no hooks):** Liella's libc provides the `libc_malloc_debug` semantics itself (`mcheck`, `mcheck_pedantic`, `mprobe`, `mcheck_check_all`, `mtrace` with `MALLOC_TRACE` read through `secure_getenv` and never written in a secure process, `M_PERTURB`): checked blocks carry 16 guard bytes before and 8 after, tracked in a library-owned table; `mcheck` succeeds only before the first block the C family hands out; a freed block reports `MCHECK_FREE`; the mtrace log follows the reference's format. Off, the cost is one relaxed load of one atomic word per call (`Heap::alloc`/`free` are `#[inline(always)]` so the check does not stop the fast path being inlined: 13.7 ns per 64-byte pair). The hook variables stay inert. `malloc_info` options other than 0 give -1 `EINVAL` (malloc_info(3), §3.2 since 2026-10-04; glibc returns 22); `malloc_trim` returns 1 only when pages were released; `mallopt` returns 0 for parameters it does not honour (D-3.4). |
| D-3.6 | §3.5 | HIST | **Internal:** `Arena` (obstack semantics) returns `Result`. **Boundary:** `obstack_alloc_failed_handler` (default: exit) is called by the legacy adapter, per the contract. |
| D-3.7 | §3.7 | HIST | The allocator never uses `brk`: pages come from `mmap` only. So `brk`/`sbrk` (thin wrappers) cannot corrupt the heap (observable: no interaction with `malloc`). |
| D-3.8 | §3.4 | HIST | `alloca` is a compiler builtin. Nothing to implement. |
| D-3.9 | §3.1 | — | **S8 is enforced by lint.** `clippy.toml` lists the infallible `alloc` methods (`Vec::push`, `with_capacity`, `reserve`, `extend_from_slice`, `insert`, `resize`, `append`, `vec![x; n]`, `Box::new`, `String::push_str`, `to_vec`, `to_owned`, `Extend::extend`, ...). Every library crate root denies `clippy::disallowed_methods` outside tests. Host tools (`xtask`, build scripts) and tests are exempt. **Accepted by the owner (2026-10-01).** **Manual review obligations**, since no lint can catch them: (1) `Iterator::collect` into a `Vec`, `String` or other collection; (2) `format!` and `alloc::fmt::format`; (3) `Clone` of a collection (`Vec`, `String`, `Box`). In library code each of these is either replaced by a fallible equivalent (`TryVec::from_slice`, `try_clone`, a fallible collect helper) or carries a comment explaining why it cannot fail. Every review of a library crate checks for all three. |
| D-3.17 | §3.1 | — | **`realloc` resizes with one lookup** (REALLOC-ONE-LOOKUP, TIMING-COV-REALLOC-GROW-NONAVX2, ruling #3389). `Heap::fit(pages, addr, size)` finds the block once, through the slab hint, and returns `Same(usable)` (the block already serves the request), `Held(Held{class, index})` (it must move; the block is already located) or `Other` (not a small block). It replaces `fits_in_place` and covers `0 < size <= MAX_SMALL` (was `<= 1 KiB`). `Heap::resize_held` moves a `Held` block without a second lookup: it takes a block from the target class with `alloc_hint`, copies, clears the old bit and calls `freed_into`; any miss falls back to `resize_slow`. `Heap::resize` is `fit`, then `resize_held` or `resize_slow`. The target size comes from `move_target`, the general path's forecast rule, which `resize_slow` now uses too, so a move copies once. Size 0 inside `resize` (reachable only through `malloc_debug`) takes `resize_slow`; the result is unchanged (class 0 stays in place, any other class gets a class 0 block). Exports: `realloc` and `__libc_realloc` return `p` with no stack frame on `Same`; `Held` goes to `realloc_held` (`#[inline(never)]`); `Other` goes to `realloc_general`. **Rules kept unchanged:** up to 1 KiB the stay-in-place rule is `HALF_BELOW` (PERF-REALLOC-USABLE-3); above 1 KiB `keeps_in_place` applies, the general path's own rule, so requests above `FORECAST_CAP` no longer take the locate, general alloc, general free route. Observable results (returned pointer, contents, `errno`) are unchanged. Was: the entry's in-place test found the block and failed, then `realloc_general` found it again in `Heap::resize` (32 B grow: 201 instructions, 59 + 130 + 12 copy; 2048 B: 467, of which 265 in `resize_slow`). Measured (`wl_percall` `realloc_grow_x2`, Broadwell-EP host, instructions per call): AVX2 dispatch glibc 199.5, before 252.9, after 209.8 (1.05 of glibc); non-AVX2 (`hwcaps=-AVX2`) before 288.8, after 245.7 (1.23); the gap left is the non-AVX2 copy of 1 to 2 KiB blocks, not changed here. Gate on 96b75b97: 8810 passed, 0 failed, conformance 11/11; four plants caught (copy one short, grow past usable, keep-big always true, alloc into the old class), free-before-copy equivalent. Not measured: wall time (timing-host jobs not run). Report: `handoff/TIMING-COV-REALLOC-GROW-NONAVX2-report.md`. |
| D-3.18 | §3.1 | — | **Small-class block index: one multiply for every class** (TIMING-COV-MALLOC-PAIR-CHAIN, 2026-11-06). Malloc's block offset stays `i * size` and free's block index stays `(off * magic) >> 40` with the start check `q * size == off`, for power-of-two classes too. A shift form for power-of-two classes (a `log2(size)` word in `FREE_VIEW`, a class-kind branch) was built and measured slower on the Haswell-EP class at default and hwcaps=-AVX2: +9 instructions and +1.4 to +1.7 cycles per malloc/free pair, heap_mix_real +7 to +9% cycles; without BMI2 a shift by a register count is 3 uops, and the shift-table load and class test add the rest. Reverted; the test `every_class_places_blocks_by_index_and_finds_them_again` (every class, indexes past one bitmap word, interior addresses at the alignment step) stays. Register: docs/saturation/04-allocator.md. |
| D-3.19 | §3.1 | — | **The heap's first reservation is one mapping** (HEAP-FIRST-USE, 2026-11-10). The first allocation of a process maps one range: the first segment (at its 16 MiB boundary), then one page holding generation 0 of the cache table, the segment bases and the segment hash, then the first 64 KiB cache chunk. Was five mappings (cache table 8 MiB, cache chunk, segment bases 8 MiB, segment hash 16 MiB, the segment), each registry page its own fault. Generation 0 of the segment registry is now at most 128 segments (2 GiB of slabs) and of the cache table at most 64 caches, with or without an address-space limit (amends D-3.14's "unlimited keeps the maxima"); later generations double as under D-3.14, so a heap past 2 GiB of slabs searches more than one hash generation on a registry lookup. If the one mapping fails, each part is mapped on its own as before; a first segment mapped for another NUMA node than the shard asking is left unused. Not changed: the `getcpu` shard choice on every slab refill (D-3.12). Tests: `the_first_allocation_reserves_one_mapping` (rt: one page request), `the_first_allocation_touches_few_pages` (core, `oracle/heap_first_faults.c`). (Amended by D-3.22.) |
| D-3.20 | §3.1 | — | **The heap asks the allowed-node set once, on its first slow path** (HEAP-FIRST-USE-2, 2026-11-10; coordinator ruling on #4168; fixes #4169). Amends D-3.12's "`Heap::set_numa(true)` is called at startup": nothing is asked at startup and nothing per allocation. The first time the heap chooses a cache or a slab (`Heap::shard_of`, slow paths only) it asks `Pages::allowed_nodes` once: in the product one `get_mempolicy(MPOL_F_MEMS_ALLOWED)` with a 1024-bit mask (`EINVAL`, a machine with nodes beyond the mask, counts as several; `ENOSYS` or any other refusal as one). More than one allowed node: NUMA placement turns on (as `Heap::set_numa(true)`) and the thread's node is read on slow paths exactly as D-3.12 says. One allowed node: shard 0, the kernel's default placement (first touch, optimal there), and the node is never read, so the vDSO `getcpu` is never resolved. An explicit `Heap::set_numa` before the first slow path takes the decision instead. Out of scope: a process whose allowed set changes after the first slow path (`set_mempolicy`, a cpuset move) keeps the decision taken then. The rseq `node_id` branch of D-3.12 is not wired in the product (the node read on several nodes is the vDSO `getcpu`); unchanged by this record. Tests (rt, the `Pages` trait's simulated topology): `one_allowed_node_never_reads_the_node`, `several_allowed_nodes_place_each_threads_slabs_on_its_node`. The vDSO lookup the node read needs (HEAP-FIRST-USE-3, #4170, ruling #4197) compares symbol and version names one byte at a time (`vdso::same_bytes`) instead of through slice equality, which lowers to the library's exported `bcmp`: that entry's first small call takes the NULL-folding decision (`vm.mmap_min_addr`, 3 system calls), so a multi-node process's first `malloc` and every process's first clock call paid for it. The guard is unchanged; the program's own first copy, fill or compare takes the decision. Test (products): `the_vdso_lookup_takes_no_folding_decision`. |
| D-3.21 | §3.1 | — | **The heap's node read takes the rseq area's `node_id` when Liella registered the area and the kernel fills it** (HEAP-RSEQ-NODE, 2026-11-14; wires the branch D-3.20 recorded as not wired, escalation #4198). Makes D-3.12's "when Liella owns the thread's registration and the kernel fills it" precise. Owned: a thread Liella created or a static program's initial thread whose descriptor's area registration succeeded (`DESC_RSEQ`), or a dynamic program's initial thread whose area Liella's `ld.so` registered at tp + `RSEQ_OFFSET`; every other thread (another C library's registration, or none) is not read. Filled: the kernel's rseq ABI puts `node_id` at offset 20 (4 bytes) and fills a field only when its feature size covers it, so the field is read only when the auxiliary vector's `AT_RSEQ_FEATURE_SIZE` (27; absent before Linux 6.3) is at least 24 and the registered length (32) reaches it; the answer is asked once per process. Otherwise the vDSO `getcpu`, as before. Slow paths only, and only when several nodes are allowed (D-3.20): one node reads no node. Tests: `rseq_node_id_is_read_only_when_the_feature_size_covers_it` (kernel), `a_registration_liella_does_not_own_is_never_read` (boundary, hosted), `several_nodes_read_the_node_from_rseq` (products: on a host with several nodes and Linux 6.3+, a thread pinned to node n > 0 takes its first block from node n with the vDSO unmapped; skipped with the reason elsewhere). |
| D-3.22 | §3.1 | KERN | **The heap's address space grows with its use** (HEAP-ADDRESS-SPACE, -2, -3; GitHub issue #21, 2026-11-17). A segment's 16 MiB window is mapped only as far as its shard hands slabs out: a new segment maps its metadata and 16 slabs (`SEG_FIRST`, 4 MiB of address space, untouched until used: the ten start-up modes of `page_faults.c` use up to 16 classes, and with 2 slabs six of them grew the segment 1 to 3 times, one `mmap` each, which put the growth code into the start-up trace and pushed `free` out of layout bin 0; with 16 none grows, strace on the Zen 1 build host, HEAP-ADDRESS-SPACE-5; ruling #6514 keeps 16: its cost is VmSize, a program's first `malloc` adds +4420 KiB of address space against the reference's +132, none of it touched, and HEAP-SPILL-COLD rechecks a smaller value once the spill exists), and the current segment grows in place by doubling, at most 8 slabs (2 MiB) per step (`Pages::grow`), before a new segment is mapped; a window whose next part is taken by another mapping ends there. Generation 0 of the large-block table is at most 256 slots (`FIRST_LARGE`, one page) with or without an address-space limit, later generations double as under D-3.14 (amends D-3.14's "unlimited keeps the maxima" for this table). The first reservation (D-3.19) is the registry page, the cache chunk and the first segment's mapped part, no longer the whole 16 MiB window; below four times a segment's first mapping (`4 * SEG_MIN`) no segment is mapped (was four whole segments, D-3.14). An address inside a registered window whose slab no cache owns is resolved by the large table (`locate_in`: the window's unmapped part can hold another mapping, a large block's too). The growth runs in one cold, out-of-line function (`grow_segment`); `alloc_small`, `refill` and `take_slab` keep their earlier code apart from the test that leaves for it (HEAP-ADDRESS-SPACE-5: growth inlined into `refill`, +688 B, and a spill parameter had overflowed layout bin 0, +1 start-up fault). Reusing freed blocks of a nearby class (the spill) is not part of this record (follow-up HEAP-SPILL-COLD). Measured with `oracle/heap_address_space.c` (the issue's program; Zen 1 build host; VmSize growth over the start of `main`, KiB): one `malloc` +16448 -> +4420 (reference +132); 200000 blocks of 96..159 bytes +32836 -> +28996 (+27984); every other one refilled with `malloc(120)` +49220 -> +39236 (+29568); a pointer array grown to 200000 by doubling `realloc` +67652 -> +41288 (+28052); the least `RLIMIT_AS` over start the program needs 67652 -> 42000 (+29568). Not changed: empty segments keep their address space (returning it needs a design for the lock-free registry readers), and the 16-byte steps of the reference's chunk sizes are not copied (a refill of class 112 holes by `malloc(120)` maps new slabs). Without the spill the refill and realloc steps and the `RLIMIT_AS` need do not yet meet the issue's targets (refill 33092, realloc 35144, need 35152 KiB, measured with the spill); ruling #6513 lands growth with use now with those bounds at the measured levels, and HEAP-SPILL-COLD closes the gap. Tests: `the_heap_keeps_address_space_near_its_use` (core: malloc1 and alloc within their measured value plus one slab, refill and realloc within their measured value, and the program under `RLIMIT_AS` = start + 42000 KiB), the rt heap tests of `heap_and_sync.rs`. Under a limit that refuses the over-mapping by the alignment, the page source places an aligned mapping exactly (HEAP-ADDRESS-SPACE-9, -10): where the kernel would put the bytes, else the aligned address just above or below; a gap that holds the bytes but no aligned range (one just above another segment) is blocked with one-page `PROT_NONE` mappings that never replace one, spaced so that no free piece fits, and the kernel is asked again, at most 8 times, the blockers removed before returning. Tests: `kernel_pages_map_aligned_under_an_address_space_limit` and `kernel_pages_map_aligned_past_a_gap_without_an_aligned_range` (boundary `s03_memory_symbols.rs`). (Amended by D-3.23, D-3.24.) |
| D-3.23 | §3.1 | — | **Under an address-space limit, a shard about to map a new segment first takes the slabs other shards hold** (HEAP-SPILL-COLD-2, ruling #7441). A thread that changes NUMA node mid-run refills from its new node's shard; with no segment there, that shard mapped one (`SEG_MIN`: 256 KiB of metadata and 16 slabs, 4352 KiB of address space) even while the first node's shard held never-used or empty slabs. Now, when the process has an `RLIMIT_AS` and another shard holds such a slab (its `empty` list or its segment's mapped, never-used part, read without that shard's lock as a hint), `new_segment` maps nothing and `refill` takes the slab through `take_elsewhere`, one shard lock at a time as before; the slab keeps its segment's home shard, so frees return it there. When the hinted slab is gone by then, the request gets a mapping of its own (`alloc_large`), as under a limit that fits no segment. Without a limit placement stays per node (D-3.12): the idle part of the second node's segment is address space only, never a touched page, and the slabs stay local to the node that uses them. The check is one cold, out-of-line function (`held_elsewhere`) called only where a segment would be mapped for a node other than the first reservation's. Measured with `oracle/heap_address_space.c` moved from the first node's CPUs to a CPU of the second at four points (the least `RLIMIT_AS` over start, KiB, fixed layout, identical on the Zen 1 and Skylake-SP build hosts, 3 of 3 runs): after malloc1 45648 -> 43600, halfway through alloc 41552 -> 41552, after alloc 41552 -> 41552, after refill 45648 -> 41296 (one node throughout: 41296 both). What is left: the second node's metadata (256 KiB, per-node segments) and, after malloc1, its new segment's 16 slabs against the 8 of the first node's next growth (+2048). Tests: `under_an_address_space_limit_a_moved_thread_takes_held_slabs_before_a_new_segment` (rt), `the_heap_bounds_address_space_after_a_node_change` (core, per move point, beside the single-node `the_heap_keeps_address_space_near_its_use`; skipped with why when the process's CPUs span one node). (Amended by D-3.24.) |
| D-3.24 | §3.1 | — | **A segment after the first reservation's maps its metadata and one growth step** (HEAP-SECOND-NODE-MAP, ruling #7494). The first reservation's segment keeps `SEG_FIRST` (16 slabs, the start-up reason in D-3.22); every later segment (a second NUMA node's, or a node's next one once its current one is spent) maps its metadata and `SEG_STEP` (8 slabs, 2304 KiB of address space with the metadata, was 4352) and grows by the same step after it, so it never holds more mapped, never-used slabs than a growing segment does. Under an address-space limit a thread that moved to a second node had needed 2048 KiB more than the first node's next growth would have taken (D-3.23's remainder). The mapping is one cold, out-of-line function (`map_later_segment`, which also makes D-3.23's `held_elsewhere` check); `take_slab` stores the slab count `new_segment` returns. Applied with and without a limit: the cost is at most one more `Pages::grow` (one system call) per later segment, which touches no page. Measured with `oracle/heap_address_space.c` on the Skylake-SP build host (two nodes; fixed layout, 3 of 3 runs, 16 KiB bisection; KiB over the start of `main`): least `RLIMIT_AS` with a move to the second node after malloc1 43600 -> 41552, halfway through alloc 41552 -> 41552, after alloc 41552 -> 41552, after refill 41296 -> 41296; one node throughout 41296 -> 41296 (the single-node bound keeps no margin); without a limit the realloc step after a move after refill 45640 -> 43592, every other step unchanged. What is left after a node change: the second node's metadata (256 KiB, per-node segments). cbench_malloc instructions per operation (base -> head, same host): the malloc_free rows 122.1 -> 122.2, lifo_batch64 8339.2 -> 8343.6, realloc_grow_16step 5722.3 -> 5725.5, the others within 0.2; layout bin 0: `refill` 3922 -> 3899 B, `alloc_slow` 1280 -> 1299 B. Tests: `a_segment_after_the_first_maps_one_growth_step_first` (rt), `the_heap_bounds_address_space_after_a_node_change` (core; its point-1 need and point-4 realloc bound tightened to the measured levels). |
| D-3.25 | §3.1 | — | **A later heap segment is placed under an address-space limit** (HEAP-FIND-DEPTH-NEED). When the over-mapping of a segment does not fit under `RLIMIT_AS`, `map_aligned_exactly` blocks the probe's gap with pages a mapping apart and asks again; it bounds the blockers per round at `EXACT_BLOCKERS`, now 9: `(align + len) / len` rounded up for a later segment (metadata and 8 slabs, 2304 KiB, D-3.24), was 8 (sized for a first segment, 5). At 8 a later segment whose aligned neighbours were taken found no range and the heap mapped per request: findutils' `find` over one directory of 200000 files (issue #21's workload) needed 37344 KiB over its 3-file need with snapshot 22.4 against 34784 with 22.3 (Zen 1 build host, find 4.9.0, tmpfs, fixed layout, `LANG=en_US.UTF-8`, 2 of 2 runs); with 9 it needs 33296 (2 of 2 runs of the test, one layout, 16 KiB grid). The locale's mappings are what take the aligned neighbours: with an empty environment the same walk needed 30080 (22.4) and 31792 (22.3), and 8 blockers were enough. A static program does not hit it (its aligned neighbours are free: 63824 KiB on both snapshots). Whether a run reaches the blocking stage depends on the layout: with next's current products the aligned slot was free and a build with 8 needed what 9 does (48592 KiB, strace: no blocker), so the blocker count is tested by layout. Tests: `kernel_pages_place_a_later_segment_when_both_aligned_slots_are_taken` (boundary `s03_memory_symbols.rs`: both aligned candidates taken, the higher gaps covered so the probe's gap is the kernel's first choice, 9 blockers needed; host and native passes) and the workload bound `find_over_200000_entries_bounds_its_address_space` (core, run in `en_US.UTF-8`; skipped, saying why, without the locale archive or with a stack hard limit too low to set the phase). That bound is taken over the layout's phase (HEAP-FIND-DEPTH-NEED-2): the need depends on where the mappings end within the heap's 16 MiB alignment, and a change in any library's size moves it. Shifting the mmap base page by page (a stack limit above 128 MiB, fixed layout) gave 33048 to 33576 KiB over 3 entries in bands 256 KiB apart, the 3-entry need constant (15276; Skylake-SP build host, page-exact, 145 shifts 32 KiB apart over the highest band). In the highest band a later segment's aligned slot has room for one growth step before another mapping, so the walk places one more segment. The test bisects each need to the page (on a 16 KiB grid the difference moved by a step between hosts whose start-up differs by a page) and samples 8 phases 2 MiB apart. A KiB bound on the need over 3 entries (33576, the worst phase measured) was crossed by unrelated changes in three trains, so the gate is a rule measured in the same run (HEAP-FIND-DEPTH-NEED-3): at each phase the walk's need under a limit is at most 548 KiB over the address space the same walk leaves mapped at exit without a limit (`VmSize`, reported by a freestanding object preloaded into every run; the heap keeps its segments, and the over-mapping it aligns them with is returned on the way). Start-up, the library's own allocations and the walk's real use are in both and cancel. The 548: under a limit a later segment may go to an aligned slot where another mapping stops its growth after one step, and the walk places one more segment, 256 KiB of metadata each; two of them, plus one round's 9 blocker pages. Measured on the Haswell-EP build host: 0 KiB over at 4 phases, 256 at 3, 264 at 1; with 8 blockers 1188 to 1444, which issue #21's formula alone (need over 3 entries at most 35000, also asserted) would pass (34932 at most). Routing the library's allocations through the heap (INTERNAL-ALLOC-ROUTING-3) left the 200000-entry need unchanged at every phase and the 3-entry need 4 KiB lower. |
